TO THE ELECTORS OF SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE.

GENTLEMEN,- As • dissolution of Parliament is imminent, I take the earliest opportunity of asking for a renewal of the impor.nt trust conGded to me in 1875. It has been my gamma endeavour during four ,essions of Parliament, by an unre- mitting attention to my duties, to show my appreciation of the high honour conferred upon on and if you again accept my aervicm, you nmy rely on my acting as here- , tofore.

Her Majesty's Government bar e received from me • very cordial support, hnving, in my judgment, : through extraordinary difficulties, conducted the foreign affairs of the nation with considerable Get and success, and by their commendable firmnews and forethought not only secured that peace which is likely to prove lasting, but extricated this country from • perilous position, which might have resulted in dreadful sear, thereby reviving that just influence in Europe which it is to desirable should be inaintained by this country.

The complications in Afghanistan and South Africa have been handled in amanitan deserving the continued cnnfldence of this nation. And the policy pronounced by Her Majesty's Government hae repeatedly received the ready and hearty support of the British Houses of Parliament. I on. in favour of

THE GZNERAL ELECTION. JOINING BATILE.

The great electoral contest of ISBO has commenced in right earnest, and all over the three kingdoms the ematending -forces am joining battle with a zeal and earnestnees that has perhaps been never before equalled on any similar occasion. The formal addressee of the several candidates to their eonsti• effects here alone supplied newspaper readers with a formidable amount of t•leetioneering literature during the week, and there in no excuse for any, save the most unlettered, remaining ignorant of the great queetions that are at issue, or of the importanes of the struggle. Sound argument, eloquence, purity of motive, and an earnest desire to do the right are the distinguishing eliaraemrintics of a large number of the Liberal addressee and speech.; while many of the Tory utterances on the other hand, from Lord Fkaeonsfield downwards, are nothing better than melfish attempts to <Lizzie the eyes of the eleetore by flaunting before them the modern phantom. of Imperialism and military glory. The aim of the Liberal parry is to lead o. hack into the paths of peace and plenty, to turn the attention of the nation from foreign dixturbancee and foreign wars to national &elf-improvement, and to point out that the only safe policy oven in times of uncertainty and disquietude is • policy of economy and retrenchment in the public expenditure and of non- interference iu quarrel, and ware that do not directly concern ua The almost avowed aim of the Tory Premier and hie obedient followers is to transform England into a great military power—regardless of expense and re- gardless of the sufferings and the misery that the carrying out of Knell a p PLC, no.tld entail upon the great bulk ef the people at home—in order that she may assume • position of " acsendency " amongst the nations. But the ascendancy " of the Empire under conditions Au. b as these would rnean the degrade- ' tion of the people. We are much mistaken if the remit of .the coming struggle will not be a very decided nega • tire on the part of the nation at large to L trd Bea- consfield's invitation to travel nay further with him in a direction, that if persevered in, must eventually lead to something very like the milimry despotism under which the German empire is now groaning. The crisis, therefore, is one the importance of which it would not be easy to exaggerate and the danger ie real.

Happily, however, there are many warning voice. in the air, and clear above them all it that of Mr. Gladstone's, who opened hie Mid• Lothian campaign in Edinburgh, on Wedneeday, in a splendid epeech on the foreign policy of the Government. The time hi gone bye ter further denunciation,. of Lori Bement:ln- field and hie Government for what they have already socompliehed, bet it it of immense importance that a oorrect estimate should he formed from hbi past eoulnet of what would be his future policy in the event of auttb•a calionity as the return of the Conserva- tive party to power. div.head: CONSERVATIVE MEETING ON THURSDAY NIGHT.
div.p: THE CONSERVATIVE MEETING ON THURSDAY NIGHT.

The Conserv:We; de-i;;;tra.t.ir; In-ibe Public Hall on Thursday night wan in some rrepeets vite as imp gtant a one as that which wee accorded to Mr. Mclifinnietr on the previous Monday. But there was one feature about the Conservative gathering that must have struck even the least observant, namely, that a very large moiety of those present were not Conservatives. They were silent listeners, probably drawn thither from feelings of curiosity to hear so great a gun as Mr. Crowe: When there were cheers the cheers were not general, and when hands were held up in favour of a reeolution, in the front gallery and other portione of the building there were large gape, as it were, where the audience appeared to sit ulmovorl, and there were no hands retard. The Liberal meeting on the other hand appeared to be thoroughly unani• mous, and there wan all that aympathy between the speakers and the audience that is absolutely necessary to the suceese of • great political gathering. At Thureday'e mooting the audience at the commeinw- :wilt was rather noisy and unruly, and the opening xpeeches, including that of Sir Gilbert Greenall, were delirered after the manner of a dumb ehow. The great event of the evening WM the speech of the Horne Secretary. He was introdueed to the meeting by Alderman J. Derive and Mr. E. J. Nicholeon, with a great If .urish of trionpete and an enumeration of all the great things ho had done for the working chows. With respect to three measur. s we may ntomerve that they are the sum total of all we have received from a Tery administration during their six years of offiae. And after all to what do they amount 'r A. Factory Act, wan • of the provisionn of which have been every questionable benefit to either manufacturers or work, people, • Masters and Workmens Act, in which there is mush room for improvement, and that ono day will have to be dealt with by a Liberal Government,the Prisons Act, and the Artisans' Dwelliugs Act, which is nearly an great a failure. Mr. Cross's Water Bill. By the way it was rather amusing to ohs era how anxious our cautious Home Secret., was to keep clear of that watery grave, where hie reputa- tion as a statelonan lire ; and, not- withstanding repeated references to it by voices in the crowd he avoided all mention of it, and turned a " deaf ear" to hin tormentor.. True to the instincts of his party and to the example met him by Lord Beaconsfield, Mr. Cross said as little as he decently could about &Atlantic legislation. The greater portion .rf his addresa was devoted to foreign affairs and a wmewhat wcarinorne defence of the foreign policy of the Government. But perhaps the moot noteworthy, as it wen also the most objsetionahle por- tion of the Home Seeretary'n speech, was the atwount lie gave of Lord Derby's neression. The Daily -Verve calls this portion of the speech an •• uneeemly ansault on Lord Derby, and then frOOK on to p dot mit that Mr. Crow owes his miniwerial career to Lord Derby. "on whose urgent representation, it is understm4, he was appointed by Lord Bsanonsfield to the Al, which he still fills." This is a well known fact in Lanesehire, and it only reqiiirre to be mentioned in order to take the cream off Mr. Alderman Davies'. grandiloquent rigmarole about the " excellency of Lord Beaconsfield " being of "the highest and bent." And that thin wonderful exrelleney lay "in his great esperience of, and hie happy selection of men." Mr. •Croon is not what anyone in their renew would demeribe as a very brilliant etatenman. But anonnit a party of mediocrities • 'IMO like the Home Secretore, because he is poriseosed of good b 1114131411 cap/wiry, is regarded as a burning and a shining light. The Tories and Alderman Davies are in the habit of regarding him as • mat fortunate arquisition, but it bright that they ehould remember that it in to Lela. Derby and not to Lord Bea...field that they are indebted for the gift. Previous to hie appointment as Home Secretary Mr. Crow was an unknown man. "The pot," says the article we have guot.d, mu far in crew. of any Parliamentary position which Mr. Crow had at that time gained ; but his administration of his department has in sores ro- mpecte justified Lord Derby's discernment of character. Of course Mr. Crow was in no may Deena to follow the author of bin political fortune, He W., on the contrary, bound hi take the coarse which his own honest judgment suggested. But it is warcely de- cent to vilify his benefactor. He speaks of Lord Derby's retirement from office 48 if it were an acted cowardice. He knows very well that it was an act of °mirage, performed under painful and trying eir- cumetancee, to which Mr. Crow endeavour. to add further bitterness. Whoever else enemies, he at least might becomiugly be silent." As to Sir Gilbert Greeriall'e epeech, what shall we 'ay of it f Wan it the special of the evening or wa. it a ?menial at all 7 He bowed and he moiled and he smiled and he bowed to a noisy crowd who had not the slightest idea of what he was trying to soy. You know who Stubs in, where he comes from. Ire. In short, an far as weer:add make Sir Gilbert out he eenaidere Stella to be the original that Lord B iwon.field had in view when he talked of man of '• leading and light " and anyone able to secure the annnort of Stub, must, as a matter of course, he returned member fir Warring- ton. Henceforth, and until their horse are crushed at Ike polling booth, rho C antervative cry ought to be not Greworill but "Slake forever."

LECITHE AT RITOCORN.-011114.011dOyPTPOillgILIPM.11r. was delivered in Brunswick school-room by the Rev. R W. Starr, of Liverpool. Mr. John Simpson presided, and there was a large attendance. The lecturer announced his subject as. "A ~rowl (torn John Bull, or the good old times," erf,l referred in an interesting inanner to the leading events of English history. The social, moral. and domestic condition of the English people front the days of the NormanNtbrough the period of the Plantagenet., and so on, to the four Georges, we. vividly portrayed. and pbovel in contrast with the present times. Having sifted the historical records for I himself, the lecturer was bound to admit:that the state of society even in the Georgian perifel wan how and ignorant. Baymg occasion to me a writing machine capable of pro- ducing several copim of the original, I have spent some time and money in a march after the fittest, and publish ray experience pro Iv. publiro. I first tried the Electric pen, which I found costly and laborious to awl. I next I made a aeries of purchases of the various Chroniographs." Thor were of various ,uality and sufficient price. Whilst I was testing them I had the masf fmtune to get h;to cm- respondence with Mr. Fkilas, the well-known consulting and analytical chemist of Turnharn Green, who had just been delivering a lecture on the general subject before the Society of Fine Art, Ile gave no the following receijd and mi- nute instructions for making the Chromograph. Take one pound of gelatine (Coignet's gold label is the heat), soak tlie dakm in 3110 larger quantity of water till they are quite mft, take diem out, pill them in a drainer for a few minutes till the surplus water him run off them, then molt in a basin over a slum bath, .Id four pounds glycerine, 0,010, and let the compound Way over the steam bath till all the water has evaporated. An ounce of acetic mid added to them proportions would be found an improvement. When the water is evaporated pour the stuff into shallow tins, and in 24 hours the Chromograph will he ready for use. In follow- ing these instructions I have made, at about the emd of two shillings a fin, ehromographs vastly superior in quality to any I have bought at from Ps. to l2a melt. Another and still totter rocess I have tried in the Trypograph recently invented by Zilecato and Wolf. This is a aimple and highly ingenious process, which effects at less cost and trouble 04, atme sort of work that is done by the electric pen. It turn. out a practically unlimited number of copies, each plainly and clearly written in indelible lila& ink. This is, of murse, more e.tnensive than the home-made Chromograph ; bet it is a sort of thing that speedily covets its own cost.

At the Widnee Police Court, on Thureday, Arthur Fowler,. formerly relieving officer to the Prescut Board of Guardia, in the Widnes district, was brought up on remand, charged with embezzling the sums of 6.13 d., 9.. and which he , stated he had paid for cab hire in rmnov log paupers to thel Workhouse and alio £25, money entrusted to hint for the purpose of being expended in the relief of the poor. Mr. Swill, St. Helene, appeared on behalf of the police, and briefly stated the particulars as to the emhezzlemeot of the various amounts. The details or to the £25 charge has al- ready appeared in our columns. Mr Swift said that in giving out-door relief a portion of it was given in kind, in the way of provisions. 'The custom was for the relieving officer, to is,oeo elip to the pauper, authotieing him to go 00 aonte provieion dealer for what he required. Mr. Fowler wae always supplied with money in advance, in order that he might not have to go on credit, to pay the provision dealers. It appeared that Fowler, after the provision dealers bad ettp- plied a number of paut,ers, was in the habit of setting the slips I root the dealers, 00th, pretence that he could not Oct the 'matey from the guardians unless he pr.lnced the slip. He had then 11,11..1 the slips to the Guardian, and entered the money in his hooks as having Leen paid. Amongst other keine, Mr. Swift referred to an amount of M IS., which the prieoner had entered as having be, paid to Mr. Francis Lawreneon. wherteur he had not paid the money.
